gloss: A living thing that grows in soil and usually has leaves and roots.
examples: I killed every *plant* I owned until somebody gave me a pothos.
She waters the *plants* on Sunday mornings.
That *plant* needs a lot more light than it's getting.

gloss: A tall plant with a woody trunk and branches.
examples: There's a huge oak *tree* in the front yard.
They planted two *trees* the year their daughter was born.
The storm knocked a *tree* down across the road.

gloss: The colored part of a plant that produces seeds.
examples: He brought her *flowers* for no particular reason.
That *flower* only opens at night.
The *flowers* on the porch are starting to wilt.

gloss: The low green plant that covers lawns and fields.
examples: Don't walk on the *grass* while it's still wet.
The *grass* is knee-high in the back.
He cuts the *grass* every other Saturday.

gloss: The part of a plant that grows underground and takes in water.
examples: The tree's *roots* cracked the sidewalk.
Cut the plant back hard but leave the *root* alone.
Ginger *root* keeps for months in the freezer.
contrast: Many Americans say *route* exactly like *root*; others say it ROWT. The plant word is always ROOT.

gloss: The main upright part of a plant that holds up the leaves and flowers.
examples: Cut the *stems* at an angle before you put them in water.
The *stem* snapped when I tried to move the pot.
Strip the lower leaves off the *stem* first.

gloss: A thick stem that supports a plant or a flower head.
examples: He chopped the celery *stalks* into sticks.
One *stalk* of corn came up in the flower bed.
The wind bent every *stalk* in the field.
contrast: The l is silent: STAWK, not STAL-k.

gloss: A part of a tree that grows out from the trunk.
examples: A *branch* came down on the power line.
The kids climbed out onto the low *branches*.
Trim that *branch* before it starts hitting the roof.

gloss: A very small thin branch.
examples: The fire caught fast once he added some dry *twigs*.
A bird was carrying a *twig* up to its nest.
She snapped a *twig* off and chewed on the end of it.

gloss: The thick main stem of a tree.
examples: Somebody carved their initials into the *trunk*.
The *trunks* were too wide to get my arms around.
Lightning split the *trunk* right down the middle.

gloss: The rough outer covering of a tree.
examples: The *bark* peels off birches in white strips.
Deer had stripped the *bark* off all the young trees.
Cinnamon comes from the *bark* of a tree.

gloss: A small swelling on a plant that will open into a leaf or flower.
examples: The *buds* are already showing on the lilac.
Don't pick it while it's still a *bud*.
Warm weather brought the *buds* out early this year.

gloss: A flower on a fruit tree or bush.
examples: The cherry *blossoms* only last about a week.
A late frost killed every *blossom* on the apple tree.
White *blossoms* covered the whole hillside.

gloss: A flower, especially on a plant grown for its flowers.
examples: The roses put out huge *blooms* in June.
One *bloom* opened overnight.
She cut a few *blooms* for the table.

gloss: One of the colored parts that make up a flower.
examples: The *petals* fell all over the counter.
He pulled one *petal* off at a time.
Rain knocked the *petals* off the tulips.

gloss: The fine yellow powder that flowers produce in order to make seeds.
examples: Everything in the driveway is coated in *pollen*.
The *pollen* count is brutal this week.
Bees carry *pollen* from one plant to the next.

gloss: The sweet liquid inside flowers that insects and birds feed on.
examples: Hummingbirds drink the *nectar* out of those red flowers.
We fill the feeder with sugar water instead of real *nectar*.
Bees turn *nectar* into honey.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The small part of a plant from which a new plant grows.
examples: Save the *seeds* and plant them next spring.
Every *seed* I put in came up.
We buy grass *seed* by the bag.

gloss: A very young plant grown from a seed.
examples: The tomato *seedlings* are ready to go outside.
Don't let a *seedling* dry out.
He started the *seedlings* under a lamp in February.

gloss: A new shoot coming up from a seed or a plant.
examples: Little green *sprouts* came up all along the row.
The potatoes in the pantry have a *sprout* on them.
You'll see the first *sprouts* in about ten days.

gloss: A young tree with a thin trunk.
examples: The deer keep eating our *saplings*.
He staked the *sapling* so the wind wouldn't take it.
A row of *saplings* runs along the fence.

gloss: The liquid that carries water and food through a plant or tree.
examples: Maple *sap* boils down into syrup.
There's *sap* all over the windshield.
Pine *sap* is almost impossible to get off your hands.

gloss: A sharp point growing on the stem of a plant.
examples: Watch the *thorns* when you're cutting roses.
A *thorn* went straight through my glove.
He stripped the *thorns* off before he wrapped them.

gloss: A round underground part of some plants that grows into a new plant.
examples: Plant the tulip *bulbs* in October.
Squirrels dug up every *bulb* I put in.
Each *bulb* goes about six inches down.

gloss: The short part of a trunk left in the ground after a tree is cut down.
examples: We're still trying to get that *stump* out.
He sat down on a *stump* to rest.
There are three *stumps* left from the old orchard.

gloss: A thick piece of a tree trunk or branch that has been cut.
examples: Throw another *log* on the fire.
We split *logs* all afternoon.
A rotten *log* was blocking the trail.

gloss: The nut of an oak tree.
examples: *Acorns* were dropping on the roof all night.
A squirrel buried an *acorn* in the flower bed.
The driveway is covered in *acorns* every fall.

gloss: The hard scaly seed case of a pine tree.
examples: The kids filled a whole bucket with *pinecones*.
She glued a *pinecone* onto the wreath.
*Pinecones* crunched under the tires.

gloss: The soft edible part inside a seed, nut, or grain.
examples: There were a few unpopped *kernels* left in the bottom.
Cut the *kernels* off the cob with a sharp knife.
Each *kernel* has to be dried before it's stored.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *colonel* (KUR-nuhl), the army officer.

gloss: The leaves of a plant or tree taken together.
examples: People drive up here just for the fall *foliage*.
Thick *foliage* hid the house from the road.
Cut the *foliage* back once it turns yellow.

gloss: The layer of leaves and branches formed by the tops of trees.
examples: Almost no light gets through the *canopy*.
Monkeys spend their whole lives up in the *canopy*.
A hole opened in the *canopy* where the tree came down.

gloss: A small round soft fruit that grows on a bush or plant.
examples: The birds got to the *berries* before we did.
Don't eat a *berry* you can't identify.
We picked *berries* along the fence all morning.

gloss: A plant with a long stem that climbs or trails along the ground.
examples: *Vines* had taken over the whole shed.
Train the *vine* up the string as it grows.
A grape *vine* runs along the back fence.

gloss: A climbing evergreen plant with dark shiny leaves.
examples: *Ivy* covers the north wall of the building.
Pull the *ivy* off before it gets into the mortar.
There's poison *ivy* right where the trail starts.

gloss: A soft green plant that grows in a flat mat on damp ground, rocks, or bark.
examples: *Moss* grows on the shady side of the roof.
The rocks down by the creek are slick with *moss*.
He scraped the *moss* off the walkway.

gloss: A plant with long feathery leaves and no flowers.
examples: A big *fern* hangs on the porch all summer.
*Ferns* grow thick along the creek.
That *fern* wants humidity, not sun.

gloss: A wild plant growing somewhere it isn't wanted.
examples: The *weeds* were back within a week.
I pulled one *weed* and found twenty more under it.
Nothing kills those *weeds* for good.

gloss: A woody plant smaller than a tree, with several stems coming from the ground.
examples: They planted low *shrubs* along the walkway.
That *shrub* needs a hard trim in the spring.
Deer will eat any *shrub* you put in.

gloss: A low thick plant with many branches.
examples: A rabbit ran under the *bush*.
The blueberry *bushes* are loaded this year.
He cut the *bushes* back to the fence line.

gloss: A row of bushes planted close together as a fence or border.
examples: The *hedge* between the two yards is six feet tall.
He trims the *hedge* twice a summer.
They put in a *hedge* for privacy.

gloss: A tree or bush that keeps its leaves or needles all year.
examples: A line of *evergreens* blocks the wind off the field.
We planted an *evergreen* where the maple used to be.
The *evergreens* look the same in January as they do in July.

gloss: A small group of trees growing together.
examples: They own an orange *grove* outside of town.
We ate lunch in a *grove* of oaks.
The old olive *groves* are still producing.

gloss: A piece of land planted with fruit trees.
examples: We drive out to the apple *orchard* every October.
His family has run the *orchard* for sixty years.
Frost hit the *orchards* hard this spring.

gloss: A piece of land where grapes are grown, usually for wine.
examples: They bought a small *vineyard* up the valley.
The *vineyards* turn gold in late October.
Every row in the *vineyard* is numbered.
contrast: Two syllables, VIN-yurd — not vine-yard, even though it's spelled with vine.

gloss: A large area thickly covered with trees.
examples: The trail runs straight through the *forest*.
A fire burned through the *forest* north of town.
*Forests* used to cover this whole ridge.

gloss: A thick tropical forest where plants grow densely.
examples: They cut a path through the *jungle* with machetes.
The back yard turns into a *jungle* by August.
*Jungles* like that get eighty inches of rain a year.

gloss: A field of grass and wildflowers.
examples: The trail opens onto a wide *meadow*.
Deer come out into the *meadow* at dusk.
They mow the *meadow* once, in late summer.

gloss: An area of short cut grass around a house or building.
examples: He cuts the *lawn* before it gets hot.
The *lawn* went completely brown in August.
Every *lawn* on this street gets watered at six in the morning.

gloss: The area of ground around a house, usually covered with grass.
examples: The kids are out in the *yard*.
We fenced the back *yard* in for the dog.
Most of the *yards* here back onto the woods.
contrast: American *yard* is what the British call a garden; in the US a garden is where you actually grow things.

gloss: A piece of ground where flowers or vegetables are grown.
examples: She's out in the *garden* every morning.
We put in a vegetable *garden* last spring.
The *gardens* behind the museum are free to walk through.

gloss: Someone who takes care of a garden, for pay or as a hobby.
examples: My grandmother was a serious *gardener*.
They hired a *gardener* to redo the beds out front.
*Gardeners* around here start their seeds in March.

gloss: The activity of growing and looking after plants in a garden.
examples: *Gardening* is the only thing that gets him outside.
She took up *gardening* after she retired.
There's a whole shelf of *gardening* books in the kitchen.

gloss: A glass or plastic building where plants are grown in a warm protected space.
examples: He built a small *greenhouse* off the side of the garage.
The tomatoes stay in the *greenhouse* until May.
Those *greenhouses* run year round.

gloss: A place where young plants and trees are grown and sold.
examples: We picked up two apple trees at the *nursery*.
The *nursery* out on Route 9 has the best perennials.
Most *nurseries* around here close down in December.

gloss: The work of designing and planting the grounds around a building.
examples: The *landscaping* out front needs to be redone.
They spent more on *landscaping* than on the deck.
Good *landscaping* adds real value to a house.

gloss: The gathering of crops, or the crops that are gathered.
examples: This year's *harvest* was the best in a decade.
Everybody in the family helps out during the *harvest*.
Two bad *harvests* in a row nearly closed the farm.

gloss: A plant grown in large amounts for food or for sale.
examples: Corn is still the main *crop* in this county.
The *crops* went in late because of all the rain.
They rotate *crops* to keep the soil healthy.

gloss: A plant grown indoors in a pot.
examples: She has forty *houseplants* in a one-bedroom apartment.
A snake plant is the easiest *houseplant* there is.
My *houseplants* barely survived the move.

gloss: A plant with thick fleshy leaves that store water.
examples: *Succulents* die faster from too much water than from too little.
He keeps a row of *succulents* on the windowsill.
That little *succulent* hasn't grown in two years.

gloss: A container, usually round, for growing a plant in.
examples: The *flowerpot* cracked over the winter.
There are empty *flowerpots* stacked up behind the shed.
Put a saucer under that *flowerpot*.

gloss: An area of ground prepared for growing flowers.
examples: He edged the *flower bed* with brick.
Weeds took over the *flower beds* while we were away.
There's a narrow *flower bed* along the front walk.

gloss: The top layer of earth in which plants grow.
examples: The *soil* here is heavy clay.
Work some compost into the *soil* first.
Nothing grows in *soil* that dry.

gloss: Loose earth or soil.
examples: There's *dirt* under his fingernails all summer.
They dumped a truckload of *dirt* in the driveway.
Pack the *dirt* down around the roots.

gloss: Decayed plant material added to soil to feed plants.
examples: We keep a bucket of scraps for the *compost*.
Mix a few inches of *compost* into each bed.
Good *compost* smells like a forest floor.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance added to soil to help plants grow.
examples: Don't put *fertilizer* down right before a storm.
He uses a slow-release *fertilizer* in the spring.
Cheap *fertilizers* can burn the roots.
contrast: American *fertilizer*, British *fertiliser* — same word, different spelling.

gloss: A layer of bark, straw, or leaves spread on soil to hold in moisture.
examples: Put down two inches of *mulch* around the shrubs.
The *mulch* keeps the weeds down.
We get *mulch* by the truckload every April.

gloss: Animal waste spread on land to make the soil richer.
examples: The whole field smelled like *manure*.
He works aged *manure* into the beds every fall.
*Manure* has to rot before you put it near plants.

gloss: A chemical used to kill insects and other pests on plants.
examples: They spray *pesticide* on the orchard twice a season.
He won't use *pesticides* anywhere near the vegetables.
Some *pesticides* stay in the soil for years.

gloss: A machine for cutting grass.
examples: The *lawn mower* won't start again.
He borrowed my *lawn mower* and never brought it back.
Both *lawn mowers* in the shed are broken.

gloss: A garden tool with a long handle and teeth, used for gathering leaves.
examples: Hand me the *rake* — these leaves are everywhere.
The *rake* is hanging on the wall in the garage.
We wore out two *rakes* that fall.
contrast: One tool is a *rake*, singular, even though Russian грабли is plural: I need a rake, not I need rakes.

gloss: A tool with a broad blade and a long handle, used for moving dirt or snow.
examples: Grab a *shovel* and give me a hand.
The *shovel* bent on the first rock he hit.
There are two *shovels* leaning against the fence.

gloss: A digging tool with a flat blade, used for turning over soil.
examples: Turn the bed over with a *spade* before you plant.
A *spade* cuts through roots better than a shovel does.
He sharpened both *spades* over the winter.

gloss: A tool with a flat blade on a long handle, used for breaking soil and cutting weeds.
examples: Take a *hoe* down the rows and knock the weeds out.
The *hoe* is a lot faster than pulling them by hand.
Both *hoes* need new handles.

gloss: A small hand tool with a curved blade for digging in a garden.
examples: She dug all the holes with a *trowel*.
I left the *trowel* out in the rain again.
You only need a *trowel* for something that small.

gloss: A small cart with one wheel and two handles, used for carrying loads in a garden.
examples: He hauled the mulch over in a *wheelbarrow*.
The *wheelbarrow* has a flat tire.
They filled three *wheelbarrows* with rocks.

gloss: A long flexible tube for carrying water.
examples: Roll up the *hose* when you're done.
The *hose* froze and split over the winter.
We ran two *hoses* out to the far bed.

gloss: A device that sprays water over a lawn or garden.
examples: The *sprinklers* come on at five in the morning.
Move the *sprinkler* over to the dry patch.
Half the *sprinklers* are pointed at the driveway.

gloss: A container with a handle and a long spout, used for watering plants.
examples: Fill the *watering can* at the spigot outside.
She keeps a small *watering can* under the sink.
Both *watering cans* are out on the porch.

gloss: Dried grass used to feed animals.
examples: They put up enough *hay* to get through the winter.
The whole barn smelled like fresh *hay*.
He hauls *hay* out to the horses every morning.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The dry stems of grain plants, used for animal bedding and for mulch.
examples: Spread *straw* over the new grass seed.
There was *straw* all over the bed of the truck.
The bar switched to paper *straws* last year.
contrast: Uncountable as солома, but countable as a drinking straw: Can we get two *straws*?

gloss: A grass grown for its grain, which is ground into flour.
examples: Miles of *wheat* on both sides of the highway.
The *wheat* came in early this year.
This bread is half *wheat* and half rye.

gloss: A tall tropical grass with hard hollow stems.
examples: *Bamboo* will take over a yard if you let it.
The floors are *bamboo*, not oak.
He built the whole fence out of *bamboo*.

gloss: Wood that has been cut into boards for building.
examples: *Lumber* prices doubled in a single year.
He picked up some *lumber* for the raised beds.
Stack the *lumber* under a tarp.
contrast: Americans say *lumber*; the British say timber.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A large hardwood tree that produces acorns.
examples: There's a two-hundred-year-old *oak* in the town square.
The *oaks* hold their leaves into December.
The table is solid *oak*.

gloss: A tree with broad leaves that turn red or orange in fall and with sweet sap.
examples: The *maple* out front is the last tree to turn.
They tap the *maples* in late February.
A *maple* seed spins like a helicopter as it falls.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: An evergreen tree with needles and cones.
examples: A stand of *pines* runs along the property line.
The whole cabin is finished in *pine*.
That *pine* dropped needles all over the deck.

gloss: A tree with thin white or silver bark that peels off in strips.
examples: Three white *birches* grow by the mailbox.
The *birch* lost a limb in the ice storm.
You can peel *birch* bark off in sheets.

gloss: A tree with long thin hanging branches, usually growing near water.
examples: A *willow* leans out over the pond.
*Willows* drink up an enormous amount of water.
They cut the *willow* back every couple of years.

gloss: A tall shade tree with rough-edged leaves.
examples: Disease killed most of the *elms* on this street.
There used to be a huge *elm* on the corner.
They're planting *elms* downtown again.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: An evergreen tree with fragrant reddish wood.
examples: The closet is lined with *cedar*.
A row of *cedars* screens the house from the road.
He built the fence out of *cedar* so it would last.

gloss: An evergreen tree with short stiff needles and hanging cones.
examples: A blue *spruce* stands at the corner of the lot.
The *spruces* were planted as a windbreak.
That *spruce* is way too big to bring inside.

gloss: An evergreen tree with flat needles, often used as a Christmas tree.
examples: We got a Douglas *fir* again this year.
The *firs* smell strongest right after they're cut.
A *fir* holds its needles longer than a spruce.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *fur*, the coat of an animal.

gloss: A tropical tree with a tall bare trunk and large leaves at the top.
examples: *Palms* line both sides of the boulevard.
The hurricane snapped a *palm* in half.
They put a *palm* in a pot next to the pool.
contrast: The l is silent: PAHM.

gloss: A tall fast-growing tree whose leaves shake in the slightest wind.
examples: A line of *poplars* runs along the drive.
The *poplar* grew twenty feet in five years.
*Poplars* don't live all that long.
contrast: Not the same word as *popular* (PAHP-yuh-lur) — poplar has one syllable fewer.

gloss: A tree with smooth gray bark and hard pale wood.
examples: Somebody carved a heart into the *beech*.
The *beeches* keep their brown leaves all winter.
That's a copper *beech*, not a maple.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *beach*, the sand by the ocean.

gloss: A tree that produces glossy brown nuts, or one of the nuts itself.
examples: They roast *chestnuts* on the corner every December.
Blight wiped out the American *chestnut*.
A *chestnut* fell right on the hood of the car.
contrast: The t in chest- is silent: CHES-nut.

gloss: A tree with dark hard wood, or the wrinkled nut it produces.
examples: The dresser is solid *walnut*.
*Walnuts* were all over the yard by October.
He cracked a *walnut* with the back of a knife.

gloss: A tree or bush with large white or pink flowers.
examples: The *magnolia* blooms before it puts out any leaves.
*Magnolias* grow everywhere down south.
A late frost browned every flower on the *magnolia*.

gloss: A flower with a strong sweet scent that grows on a thorny bush.
examples: He sent a dozen *roses* to her office.
The *rose* by the gate blooms all summer.
*Roses* need a lot more water than people think.

gloss: A brightly colored cup-shaped spring flower that grows from a bulb.
examples: The *tulips* came up right through the snow.
She bought a bunch of *tulips* at the market.
Every *tulip* in the bed is red except one.

gloss: A small flower with white petals around a yellow center.
examples: *Daisies* grow wild along the fence.
She picked a *daisy* and stuck it behind her ear.
There was a jar of *daisies* on the kitchen table.

gloss: A large flower with curved petals, grown from a bulb.
examples: The *lilies* open a few days after you cut them.
One *lily* can scent a whole room.
Pull the pollen out of *lilies* or it stains everything.

gloss: A flower with unusually shaped petals, often grown indoors in a pot.
examples: That *orchid* has been alive for six years.
*Orchids* die from overwatering more than anything else.
He gave her an *orchid* instead of cut flowers.
contrast: The ch is pronounced like k: OR-kid.

gloss: A very tall plant with a large yellow flower and edible seeds.
examples: The *sunflowers* got taller than the fence.
A single *sunflower* in a vase is plenty.
They grow *sunflowers* out here for the oil.

gloss: A yellow spring flower with a trumpet-shaped center, grown from a bulb.
examples: *Daffodils* are the first thing up in March.
He planted two hundred *daffodils* along the drive.
The *daffodil* came up but never opened.

gloss: A small purple or blue flower that grows low to the ground.
examples: *Violets* spread through the whole lawn.
She keeps an African *violet* on the windowsill.
A few *violets* came up between the stones.

gloss: A flower with thin bright red or orange petals.
examples: Whole fields of *poppies* open in May.
A single *poppy* came up in the gravel.
The *poppies* only last a day or two.

gloss: A flower with ruffled petals and a spicy smell, common in bouquets.
examples: They dyed the *carnations* blue for the dance.
*Carnations* last a lot longer in a vase than roses.
He wore a white *carnation* on his lapel.

gloss: A bush with clusters of small purple or white flowers and a strong scent.
examples: The *lilac* by the back door blooms for about two weeks.
You can smell the *lilacs* from the street.
She cut an armful of *lilac* for the table.

gloss: A low bush with narrow gray-green leaves and fragrant purple flowers.
examples: There's *lavender* planted all along the walk.
She dries *lavender* and puts it in the drawers.
Bees are all over the *lavender* in July.

gloss: A common weed with a yellow flower that turns into a ball of white seeds.
examples: The whole yard is *dandelions* by the middle of May.
He blew the seeds off a *dandelion*.
You can eat *dandelion* greens in a salad.

gloss: A low plant with three round leaves on each stem, common in lawns.
examples: There's more *clover* in the lawn than grass.
She spent an hour looking for a four-leaf *clover*.
Bees work the *clover* all afternoon.
contrast: Don't confuse *clover* (the plant) with *clove* (the spice, or a piece of garlic).

gloss: A flower that grows on its own, without being planted.
examples: The *wildflowers* along the highway are seeded on purpose.
We hiked up to see the *wildflowers* in June.
He couldn't name a single *wildflower*.

gloss: A round full flower that blooms in the fall.
examples: Every porch on the block has *chrysanthemums* in October.
She bought one *chrysanthemum* in a pot.
The *chrysanthemums* held up through the first frost.
contrast: The ch is pronounced like k, and the stress falls on the second syllable: krih-SAN-thuh-muhm.

gloss: A bunch of flowers arranged and tied together.
examples: She caught the *bouquet* at the wedding.
He showed up with a *bouquet* and an apology.
They deliver *bouquets* the same day.
contrast: The t is silent and the stress is on the second syllable: boh-KAY.

gloss: A ring of leaves or flowers used as a decoration.
examples: There's a *wreath* on every door on the street.
She made the *wreath* out of pine and holly.
The *wreaths* go up right after Thanksgiving.
contrast: The w is silent: REETH. The plural is voiced, REETHZ.

gloss: A plant whose leaves are used to flavor food or as medicine.
examples: She grows *herbs* in a box on the fire escape.
Add the fresh *herbs* at the very end.
Basil is the one *herb* I can't keep alive.
contrast: In American English the h is silent: URB. The British pronounce it HURB.

gloss: A herb with a strong fresh taste, used in food and drinks.
examples: *Mint* will take over any bed you put it in.
He crushed some *mint* into the bottom of the glass.
There's wild *mint* growing down by the creek.

gloss: A herb with soft green leaves, used a lot in Italian cooking.
examples: Tear the *basil* instead of cutting it.
The *basil* bolted in the heat.
It takes a lot of *basil* to make pesto.
contrast: Americans say BAY-zuhl; the British say BAZ-il.

gloss: A herb with curly or flat green leaves, used in cooking and as a garnish.
examples: Chop the *parsley* fine.
Flat-leaf *parsley* has more flavor than the curly kind.
There's *parsley* growing in the window box.

gloss: A herb with stiff needle-like leaves and a strong piney smell.
examples: Throw some *rosemary* in with the potatoes.
The *rosemary* survived the whole winter outside.
He rubbed the chicken with oil and *rosemary*.

gloss: A herb with tiny leaves, used to season meat and soups.
examples: A little *thyme* goes a long way.
There's *thyme* growing between the paving stones.
Strip the *thyme* off the stem with your fingers.
contrast: Pronounced exactly like *time* — the h is silent.

gloss: A herb with soft gray-green leaves, used in stuffing and sausage.
examples: The stuffing needs more *sage*.
*Sage* grows like a weed once it's established.
He fried a few leaves of *sage* in butter.
